A1.justification: Both PDFs are complete, readable 11-page versions of BioHiCL. Their text, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–C support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original retrieval, sentence-similarity, and question-answering experiments, component ablations, hyperparameter analysis, and efficiency measurements.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds results from repeated BioHiCL fine-tuning runs in Appendix B.4 and Table 5.

M1.justification: Section 2 retains the same ancestor-expanded, depth-weighted MeSH representations, regression and contrastive objectives, BGE backbones, and LoRA adaptation procedure.

E1.justification: Training, validation, and evaluation coverage is unchanged: BioASQ, TREC-CT, four IR benchmarks, BIOSSES and SciFact sentence similarity, and PubMedQA. The new variability results use the existing four IR benchmarks.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged in the main evaluation, additional fine-tuning comparisons, and efficiency analysis. New Table 5 reports only the two existing BioHiCL variants.

E3.justification: The stated data splits, metrics, model sizes, and training and evaluation settings remain unchanged. Appendix B.4 adds seed repetitions and uncertainty estimation without reporting a separate change to the evaluation design.

E4.justification: Appendix B.4 adds a limited examination of training variability across random seeds for both BioHiCL sizes on the existing IR benchmarks. The component ablations, alternative-backbone analysis, hyperparameter sweep, and efficiency analysis are retained.

E5.justification: v1 reports point scores without run counts or confidence intervals. v2 introduces repeated-run means and 95% t-based confidence intervals across the primary IR evaluation. However, B.4 states three independent runs while B.4 and Table 5 specify four degrees of freedom; three runs would ordinarily require two. This newly reports repetition without establishing an increase from a previously stated run count.

E6.justification: New Table 5 adds repeated-run summaries, including IR averages of 0.543 ± 0.005 for BioHiCL-Base and 0.532 ± 0.005 for BioHiCL-Large. Table 1 retains its checkpoint scores of 0.543 and 0.534, respectively. All previously reported results remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, hierarchical similarity construction, and Equations 1–5 are unchanged. No theorem, proof, or derivation is added; the new confidence-interval procedure concerns statistical reporting.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about hierarchical MeSH supervision, effectiveness across biomedical tasks, and computational efficiency.

C2.justification: Interpretations of component effects, prompting sensitivity, backbone adaptation, and efficiency are retained, as are the limitations concerning hierarchical-label availability and semantic specificity. B.4 adds reporting details without a new substantive interpretation or limitation.

D1.justification: Appendix B.4 newly clarifies that Table 1's BioHiCL results come from the publicly released checkpoint, distinguishing their provenance from the repeated-run summaries. Existing implementation settings and code/model access information remain unchanged.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion, cited works, and positioning of MeSH supervision relative to prior biomedical retrieval methods are unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 adds the short Appendix B.4 subsection and an explicit Table 1 reference in Section 3.2. Apart from these additions and the version/date stamp, the narrative and section organization are retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds the training-variability Table 5, moves the unchanged hyperparameter Table 4 from page 10 to page 9, and locally reflows appendix text and footnotes. The efficiency table becomes Table 6. Existing figures and table designs are retained.

improvement.justification: The repeated-run summaries and checkpoint provenance provide useful additional information, but the principal new uncertainty evidence is internally inconsistent: three runs are reported alongside t-distribution degrees of freedom of four. Without clarification or individual-run results, the reliability of the claimed 95% intervals is unresolved. Since the method and existing evidence otherwise remain unchanged, a reliable net quality improvement cannot be established.
